facts.claim: Training with the Adam optimiser in mixed precision (16-bit numbers for the maths, 32-bit for the updates) takes 16 bytes per parameter: 2 for the weights, 2 for the gradients and 12 for the optimiser’s 32-bit copy of the weights and its two running averages (Rajbhandari et al., 2020, the ZeRO paper).

ZeRO shares out the optimiser state across the data-parallel copies (stage 1, 4× less memory), then the gradients too (stage 2, 8×), then the weights (stage 3, less with every copy added); stages 1 and 2 send no more than plain data parallel, stage 3 sends 1.5× as much (Rajbhandari et al., 2020).
By the ZeRO paper’s count, GPT-2 with 1.5 billion parameters needs at least 24 GB to train with mixed-precision Adam, though its 16-bit weights alone take 3 GB (Rajbhandari et al., 2020).

Korthikanti et al. (2022) count what a transformer layer keeps for the way back at s·b·h·(34 + 5·a·s/h) bytes, for s tokens in a sequence, b sequences, a hidden size of h numbers and a attention heads; with the layer split t ways and the attention scores worked out again on the way back, it drops to 34·s·b·h/t.

Patarasuk and Yuan (2009) proved that when N computers each end with the sum of everyone’s data, at least one must pass on about 2(N − 1)/N times its own data, and gave a ring that sends exactly that: no way of summing sends less.

GPipe splits a model into K stages on K chips and each batch into M micro-batches; the idle share, the bubble, goes as (K − 1)/(M + K − 1), and was small enough to ignore once M ≥ 4×K (Huang et al., 2019).
Megatron-LM splits each transformer layer across chips with only two all-reduces in the forward pass and two in the backward pass (Shoeybi et al., 2019).

Splitting inside a layer should generally go up to the number of GPUs in one server, with pipeline stages across servers; the authors trained a 1-trillion-parameter model this way on 3,072 GPUs at 502 petaFLOP/s, 502 thousand trillion sums a second (Narayanan et al., 2021).
NVIDIA lists the H100 SXM chip with 80 GB of memory (vendor-reported, NVIDIA’s H100 page, checked 2026-10-30).

NVIDIA lists the H100 SXM at 1,979 teraFLOPS (trillion sums a second) on 16-bit numbers, a figure it gives with sparsity, a shortcut that skips zeros, and twice its rate without it (vendor-reported, NVIDIA’s H100 page, checked 2026-10-30).
Inside a DGX H100 box, eight H100 GPUs talk over NVIDIA’s fast chip-to-chip links at 900 GB/s per GPU (vendor-reported, NVIDIA’s DGX H100 user guide, checked 2026-10-30).

Between boxes, each of a DGX H100’s eight GPUs has its own network card at up to 400 Gb/s, or 50 GB/s (vendor-reported, NVIDIA’s DGX H100 user guide, checked 2026-10-30); Llama 3’s clusters also used 400 Gbps links between GPUs.
Meta’s Llama 3 70B has 80 layers, a model dimension of 8,192 and 64 attention heads (Llama 3 paper, 2024).
Llama 3 405B began pre-training with batches of 4M tokens in sequences of 4,096 tokens (Llama 3 paper, 2024).
Meta reports using 38–43% of the GPUs’ peak 16-bit speed while training Llama 3 405B on 8,192 to 16,384 H100s (Llama 3 paper, 2024).

Meta trained Llama 3 405B on 8,192 H100s with each layer split 8 ways inside a server, 16 pipeline stages and 64 copies that share out their training state, using 43% of the chips’ peak (Llama 3 paper, 2024).

Over a 54-day stretch of Llama 3 405B’s pre-training on up to 16,384 H100s, Meta counted 466 job interruptions, 419 of them unexpected, GPU issues the largest share (58.7%), and still kept over 90% of the time training (Llama 3 paper, 2024).
Young (1974) gave the best time between checkpoints as about √(2δM), for δ the time to write one and M the mean time between failures.
Daly (2006) refined Young’s interval with a closer estimate that also counts the time to restart.
